extraction.name: POPE (Polling-based Object Probing Evaluation)
extraction.description: POPE is a polling-based query evaluation benchmark designed to evaluate object hallucination in Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs). It formulates evaluation as a binary classification task prompting LVLMs with Yes-or-No questions about whether specific objects exist in an image, utilizing Random, Popular, and Adversarial negative object sampling strategies.
extraction.creator: Yifan Li, Yifan Du, Kun Zhou, Jinpeng Wang, Wayne Xin Zhao, Ji-Rong Wen
extraction.rai:dataCollection: POPE constructs evaluation triples consisting of an image, multiple questions, and binary Yes/No ground-truth answers. Ground-truth objects in the image are obtained either from existing dataset annotations (MSCOCO) or via automatic segmentation tools (SEEM). Nonexistent objects are generated using three negative sampling strategies (Random, Popular, and Adversarial). For the MSCOCO validation set, 500 images with more than 3 ground-truth objects were sampled, and 6 questions per image were generated with a balanced 1:1 ratio between ground-truth and nonexistent objects.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionType: Secondary Data analysis, Software Collection, Experiments
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Images and annotations from the MSCOCO validation set, A-OKVQA, and GQA datasets.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Images containing more than 3 ground-truth objects were selected (500 images randomly chosen from the MSCOCO validation set). For each image, 6 binary questions were created ensuring a 1:1 ratio between ground-truth and nonexistent objects for label balance. In unannotated datasets (A-OKVQA and GQA), segmentation masks and labels were extracted using SEEM before question construction.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Questions are generated following predefined natural language templates (e.g., 'Is there a/an <object> in the image?'). Ground-truth objects are assigned the label 'Yes', while negative objects selected through random, popular, or adversarial sampling strategies are assigned the label 'No'.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Validation of annotation consistency was conducted by examining the correlation between model Yes/No responses in POPE and presence of objects in model-generated captions, showing strong agreement (e.g., objects answered with 'No' were almost never referenced in generated captions).
extraction.rai:machineAnnotationTools: SEEM (Segment Everything Everywhere All at Once), ChatGPT
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: Addresses safety and reliability concerns of deploying LVLMs in real-world applications (such as autonomous driving systems, where incorrect scene understanding could lead to serious safety accidents) by providing a benchmark to measure and mitigate object hallucination.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: Visual instruction datasets exhibit an unbalanced object distribution where frequent objects dominate; models trained on these datasets inherit severe biases toward frequently appearing objects and co-occurring object groups. Models also display an overconfidence bias, heavily skewed toward answering 'Yes'.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: Only evaluates coarse-grained object hallucinations, omitting fine-grained attributes like number, attributes, and object positions; evaluated only on subsets of dataset splits due to computational constraints; relies on matching-based parsing for 'Yes' or 'No', which can fail if models provide open-ended responses; labels derived from automatic segmentation tools like SEEM can diverge from human annotations.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Testing and evaluating object hallucination in Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs).
